newsitem.title: UK: Coffee futures soar, roasters mull retail rise.
newsitem.headline: Coffee futures soar, roasters mull retail rise.

text.p: Skyrocketing world coffee prices gained more than five per cent in value to $1,630 a tonne on Thursday on news that producer nations meeting in Brazil had put together an accord to curb exports by one million bags.
They eased slightly in late European business on profit-taking and as players awaited further news from the meeting of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries.
Robusta coffee futures for March delivery edged back to around $1,570, still almost $30 up on the day, by 1615 GMT.

Current values are up 30 percent from the final trading day of 1996. Analysts said further advance was likely against a backdrop of tight stocks and producer action to curb supply and lock in firmer values.
"Rapid progress has occurred and although the market is overbought, the present rise should run as far as the August 1996 highs, at least," David Charters of Investment Research of Cambridge said.
Coffee peaked at $1,648 last August on frost scare in Brazil.
"People are just reluctant to sell the market now...certainly they are not going to go short because it is very difficult to try to pick the top the whole time," said one trader.
Thursday's new advance was propelled by news that Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) members had agreed to cut exports between January and June this year by at least one million bags.

Ugandan Trade Minister Abel Rwendeire said members had already agreed to the minimum cut and that Thursday would be spent finalising details. He said the cuts would involve both arabica types and robusta coffee, although mainly robustas.
African producers had earlier said they wanted a 2.5 million bag reduction in ACPC exports, which under a plan agreed in London in May last year already should not exceed 26.28 million bags.
A continuing dockworkers' strike in another key grower, Colombia, and prospects of lower supplies from other central and south American origins also lent support to the market.
"The market is certainly concerned with short term supply availability," UK brokerage GNI said.
The soaring cost of coffee beans has already forced at least one German coffee roaster to hike retail prices from February.
A Finnish firm, Gustav Paulig, said it would also consider a similar move if the price rise continued.
Nestle and other major European roasters said they had no immediate plans to raise prices at the supermarket but they were watching the market very closely.
